why.Depot Creek from the Canadian side: Usually the shortest way, but it crosses into the United States on foot away from a port of entry, which is not permitted.

review.notes: Depot Creek is the most used but enters the US on foot off a port of entry; NPS says crossings must be through a designated port of entry and GAO says any other land entry is illegal. Mark moved to the lawful Silver Creek way.

wa_mount_spickard_silver_glacier.primary: From Ross Lake by boat and up Silver Creek to the lake basin camp

review.notes: Depot Creek is the usual way but walks across the border at the boundary obelisk, not a port of entry; mark moved to the lawful Ross Lake and Silver Creek way.

wa_mount_spickard_southwest.primary: From Ross Lake by boat and up Silver Creek to the lake basin

why.Depot Creek from the north side of the b: Usually the shortest way, but it crosses into the United States on foot away from a port of entry, which is not permitted.

review.notes: Depot Creek is the usual way but walks across the border at the boundary obelisk, not a port of entry; mark moved to the lawful Ross Lake and Silver Creek way.

why.Two camps: the lake basin or the glacier: When the glacier is in good shape and the weather is settled, a party moves up to the saddle camp for a much shorter summit day instead of staying at the lake.

review.notes: Stored primary (Depot Creek) crosses the border on foot off a port of entry, so it must not be Most used. The only other stored way is a camp choice on the same Canadian-side approach, not a lawful way in, so no mark can be moved. Owner: clear the mark or add a lawful approach.

why.From the Chilliwack Lake road on the Can: Normally the shortest way in, but it crosses into the United States on foot away from a port of entry, which is not permitted.

review.notes: Primary is the lawful Hannegan Pass approach; the Canadian-side way is shorter but not lawful on foot off a port of entry. Keep.

why.From the Chilliwack Lake road on the Can: Normally the shortest way in, but it crosses into the United States on foot away from a port of entry, which is not permitted.

review.notes: Primary is the lawful Hannegan Pass approach; keep. Why line made plain about the border.

why.Provincial park approach from the north: Walks in from the Canadian provincial park over Frosty Mountain, but it crosses into the United States on foot away from a port of entry, which is not permitted.
why.Pacific Crest Trail north from Harts Pas: When no boat is available and you want to stay in the United States; it is about 27 miles each way along the crest from Harts Pass, which usually opens only in July.

review.notes: Primary is the all-US Ross Lake boat approach; sources describe it as the lawful route, so keep. Frosty Mountain way is unlawful on foot off a port of entry and was never primary.

why.Provincial park approach from the north: Walks in from the Canadian provincial park over Frosty Mountain, but it crosses into the United States on foot away from a port of entry, which is not permitted.
why.Pacific Crest Trail north from Harts Pas: When you have no boat or water taxi and will walk the roughly 27 miles of crest in, after the Harts Pass road opens, usually in July.

review.notes: No two sources show the PCT as more used than the boat approach; keep. Frosty Mountain way is unlawful off a port of entry.

wa_liberty_cap_ptarmigan_ridge_finish.primary: White River, St. Elmo Pass and across the Carbon

why.Mowich Lake, Spray Park and the Ptarmiga: Only if the Mowich Lake road reopens, for the prettier walk that reaches the ridge from the bottom; it needs a car shuttle to the White River end, where the Emmons descent comes out.

review.notes: Mowich Lake road has no public access (NPS road status, Oct 2026); recent reports and Mountain Project say Ptarmigan Ridge must be reached from White River. Mark moved.

why.Mowich Lake and Spray Park: Only if the Mowich Lake road reopens, for a shorter walk in; it needs a car shuttle to the White River end, since the usual descent comes out there.

review.notes: White River already marked and is the only reachable start now. Mowich line rewritten because its road is closed.
Sources split: Mountain Project lists both approaches without ranking; some favour the south side later in summer. No two sources agree on a move.
Day trips and overnights at the bench are both common in recent reports; split, so keep.

why.North Fork Sauk / Cougar Creek (FR 49): Later in July and August when the river is low, or when the rough spur to the Bedal trailhead is impassable; the traditional approach, but with log crossings and brushy tread.

review.notes: Bedal Creek increasingly preferred, Cougar Creek the traditional standard; Bedal mark stays.
One source calls summer the usual season, others praise the early-season snow ascent; both ways are the same Lena Lake approach. One source is not enough to move.

why.Dosewallips roadbed, Lake Constance trai: For parties without a bike, or who prefer to walk the five miles of closed road; it adds hours to the day at both ends.

review.notes: Three independent accounts (including a Sept 2026 trip) ride bikes up the closed road; one calls biking highly recommended.
Route shares the West Face approach; no source ranks the two ways in, so keep.
No evidence that the centre-route start is more used than the gully ledge; keep.
